title: The fire that didn't burn
hookLine: a messenger gives the most powerful king in the world good advice, and the king answers by setting the messenger's tail on fire
carry: sita's prayer: holding someone up from afar

cards: Hanuman stands tied up before Ravana's throne, and the first thing Valmiki tells us is that Hanuman is impressed. Ravana is magnificent: radiant, crowned, mighty, surrounded by ministers.
Hanuman thinks that if this king weren't so unrighteous, he could be the guardian of heaven itself. A minister asks who sent him, and Hanuman answers. Not with threats.

teach.b: I am Sugriva's envoy, he says, and Rama's messenger. Then he speaks to Ravana as to a king who could still choose well. You know dharma.
You've gained great power through austerities. Don't throw it away for another man's wife. Give Sita back to Rama, and you can still live.

teach.h: AN ENVOY MAY NOT BE KILLED.
teach.b: Ravana's answer is rage: kill him. Then his younger brother Vibhishana speaks up. It is against dharma to kill a messenger.
Punish him some other way. Ravana gives in, grudgingly. A monkey's tail is precious to him, he says.
Set it on fire. So they wrap Hanuman's tail in old cloth, soak it in oil, light it, and parade him through the streets with drums. The rakshasi guards run to tell Sita.

teach.h: SITA PRAYS TO AGNI FROM AFAR.
teach.b: And Sita, in the grove, turns to the fire god, Agni. If I have served my husband faithfully, she prays, if I have any merit at all, be cool to Hanuman.

teach.h: THE FIRE DOES NOT BURN HIM.
teach.b: The fire, burning brightly on his tail, does not burn him. Hanuman is astonished, and guesses it's Sita's doing, or Rama's power, or his father the wind's friendship with fire. Look at Sita here.
She can't reach Hanuman. She can't fight for him. She can only pray from where she sits, and in the story, that holds him up.
This is one of the quiet practices of Hindu life: praying for someone you can't reach, often with a small lamp lit at home for someone far away or in a hospital.

how: The burning of Hanuman's tail and Sita's prayer to Agni are familiar scenes in Ramayana retellings; many Hindu families light a diya at home and pray for someone ill or far away, and Vibhishana's rule that an envoy must not be killed is cited by some teachers as dharma in war.

o: Hanuman's tail set alight, and the fire that doesn't hurt him
the fire sacrifice Rama makes before he crosses the sea

s: Hanuman threatens Ravana from the start
he advises him to return Sita and save himself.
Vibhishana argues that killing an envoy is against dharma
so Ravana orders a different punishment.
Sita asks Agni to be cool to him, and the fire doesn't hurt.

games.q: you're Vibhishana. your brother the king orders an envoy killed. what do you say?
o: killing an envoy is against dharma; punish him another way.
games.why: Vibhishana tells Ravana that an envoy must never be killed, whatever he says. Ravana settles for burning his tail.

practice: If you pray, light a small lamp or candle, or simply fold your hands, and name someone going through a fire right now: an illness, a hard week, a trial. Sita couldn't go to Hanuman; she prayed from where she was.
Offer them to God in your own way. If you don't pray, send them coolness and steadiness with each breath out, and then send them a real message if you can.

wordCard.voice: The burning. Ravana rejects Hanuman's counsel, Vibhishana saves the envoy's life, and Hanuman's tail is set alight, but Sita asks the fire to be cool, and it is.

orig.note: Sanskrit agni, fire, and the god of fire, whom Sita asks to be cool.

carryVoice: Your line: sita's prayer: holding someone up from afar. Tomorrow, the fire spreads across Lanka. Rest well.
